By exploring how model forecast errors relate to properties of the air-sea interface, we infer what ocean information these atmospheric emulators are able to derive from atmospheric data alone, and what they cannot. This highlights the regions and processes through which the ocean independently influences the atmosphere on fast timescales. We perform this analysis for GraphCast, finding clear relationships between air-sea properties and the forecast errors over the ocean, including clear seasonal effects. We then explore what this reveals about GraphCast's internal representation of the ocean. In addition to understanding real-world ocean-atmosphere interactions, this analysis provides guidance for improving forecast skill and physical realism in MLWP models, and for informing how future machine learning models should use ocean information on short timescales.

papers.title: Finding the right XAI method -- A Guide for the Evaluation and Ranking of Explainable AI Methods in Climate Science
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and compare different XAI methods in climate science to choose the most suitable one for a specific task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for evaluating and ranking XAI methods in climate science, enabling researchers to choose the most suitable method based on properties like robustness, faithfulness, complexity, localization, and randomization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that evaluating XAI methods using multiple properties is essential for selecting the right method in climate science, and the proposed framework aids in this process.
papers.key_findings:
Salience methods (Integrated Gradients, input times gradient, LRP) show higher faithfulness and complexity, while sensitivity methods (gradient, SmoothGrad, NoiseGrad, FusionGrad) are more robust to parameter randomization.
Explanation methods exhibit architecture-dependent performance differences in robustness, complexity, and localization.
LRP-composite provides a trade-off between faithfulness and interpretability, yielding high robustness but lower faithfulness.
The evaluation framework allows practitioners to rank XAI methods based on task-specific requirements.
The study highlights the importance of evaluating XAI methods in the absence of ground truth explanations.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is based on a single case study, which may limit generalizability.
The choice of baseline for Integrated Gradients and DeepSHAP (all-zero maps) may affect explanation performance.
The region of interest for localization might not be optimally chosen.
future_direction: Extend the evaluation to other climate tasks, networks, and explanation methods.
Incorporate human evaluation to assess the usefulness of explanations for climate scientists.
papers.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods shed light on the predictions of machine learning algorithms. Several different approaches exist and have already been applied in climate science. However, usually missing ground truth explanations complicate their evaluation and comparison, subsequently impeding the choice of the XAI method. Therefore, in this work, we introduce XAI evaluation in the climate context and discuss different desired explanation properties, namely robustness, faithfulness, randomization, complexity, and localization. To this end, we chose previous work as a case study where the decade of annual-mean temperature maps is predicted. After training both a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), multiple XAI methods are applied and their skill scores in reference to a random uniform explanation are calculated for each property. Independent of the network, we find that XAI methods Integrated Gradients, layer-wise relevance propagation, and input times gradients exhibit considerable robustness, faithfulness, and complexity while sacrificing randomization performance. Sensitivity methods -- gradient, SmoothGrad, NoiseGrad, and FusionGrad, match the robustness skill but sacrifice faithfulness and complexity for randomization skill. We find architecture-dependent performance differences regarding robustness, complexity and localization skills of different XAI methods, highlighting the necessity for research task-specific evaluation. Overall, our work offers an overview of different evaluation properties in the climate science context and shows how to compare and benchmark different explanation methods, assessing their suitability based on strengths and weaknesses, for the specific research problem at hand. By that, we aim to support climate researchers in the selection of a suitable XAI method.

papers.title: Learning from nature: insights into GraphDOP's representations of the Earth System
papers.research_question: How does the GraphDOP model, trained solely on meteorological observations, develop internal representations of the Earth System state, structure, dynamics, and observing system characteristics?
papers.core_contribution: The GraphDOP model, trained exclusively on Earth System observations without prior physical knowledge, develops coherent internal representations (a 'world model') of the underlying physical state, viewing effects, and meteorological dynamics to successfully predict future observations.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained purely on observations of the Earth System can develop internal representations of the physical world, including state, dynamics, and observing system characteristics, providing a foundation for future data-driven weather prediction models.
papers.key_findings:
GraphDOP constructs a unified latent representation of the Earth System state that is common across diverse observation types, such as cloud structures being consistent in predictions for satellite radiances and in-situ cloud fraction measurements.
The model learns to emulate complex viewing effects, such as limb effects in microwave sounders and sunglint in visible imagery, mapping from its latent state to observed variables.
GraphDOP develops internal representations of meteorological structures and dynamics, enabling it to infer unobserved, non-local variables (e.g., jet streams, surface pressure) from limited input observations, such as from a single geostationary satellite.
In the absence of input observations, the model's predictions revert to a learned climatological prior, demonstrating the role of learned priors in its inference.
The model captures the complex dynamics of extra-tropical weather systems, including rapid cyclogenesis, with skill approaching physics-based systems.
papers.limitation:
The current GraphDOP configuration is restricted to using only 12 hours of observations as input, with no background state provided.
It remains an open question whether external bias correction schemes are necessary or if the model can learn to correct for systematic observation errors internally.
Questions remain over whether the observational coverage is sufficiently complete to provide enough constraint for observation-only approaches to reach their full potential.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence and cycle through several input windows, carrying information forward via the latent space to provide a prior estimate of the current state.
Investigate the model's handling of systematic observation errors to determine if external bias correction is necessary.
Explore whether longer input windows or cycling information from earlier windows can extend the area of skillful predictions beyond directly observed regions.
papers.abstract: Through a series of experiments, we provide evidence that the GraphDOP model - trained solely on meteorological observations, using no prior knowledge - develops internal representations of the Earth System state, structure and dynamics as well as the characteristics of different observing systems. Firstly, we demonstrate that the network constructs a unified latent representation of the Earth System state which is common across different observation types. For example, cloud structures maintain physical consistency whether viewed in predictions for satellite radiances from different sensors, or for direct in-situ measurements of the cloud fraction. Secondly, we show examples that suggest that the network learns to emulate viewing effects - learned observation operators that map from the unified state representation to observed properties. Microwave sounder limb effects and geometric viewing effects, such as sunglint in visible imagery, are both well captured. Finally, we demonstrate that the model develops rich internal representations of the structure of meteorological systems and their dynamics. For instance, when the network is only provided with observations from a single infrared instrument, it is able to infer unobserved, non-local structures such as jet streams, surface pressure patterns and warm and cold air masses associated with synoptic systems. This work provides insights into how neural networks trained solely on observations of the Earth System spontaneously develop coherent internal representations of the physical world in order to meet the training objective - enhancing our understanding and guiding future development of these models.

papers.title: Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features
papers.research_question: Whether interpretable abstractions corresponding to physical features are present in the internal representations of data-driven physics models like GraphCast, and if these abstractions are physically consistent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable physical features from the internal activations of the data-driven weather model GraphCast, and that modifying these features leads to physically consistent changes in predictions, offering a window into the model's black-box behavior.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders applied to GraphCast extract highly interpretable physical features, and modifying these features allows probing of the model's internal abstractions, contributing to model trust and potential scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features in GraphCast corresponding to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal/seasonal patterns, precipitation, geographical coding, and sea-ice extent.
Features like sea-ice extent are learned dynamically even though not present in the model's input or output.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are identified, reflecting potential architecture bias.
Sparse probing identifies single features that strongly predict tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
Interventions that modify a tropical cyclone feature lead to interpretable and physically consistent changes in hurricane strength and evolution in the model's predictions.
papers.limitation:
The correlation between sea-ice features and actual ice extent is demonstrated, but a more rigorous causal analysis is needed for a complete account.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are spurious and potentially undesirable from an interpretability perspective.
ERA5 fields themselves are not in perfect hydrostatic balance, which affects the evaluation of physical consistency.
future_direction: Conduct more rigorous causal analysis of the discovered features.
Build mechanistic accounts for the interaction of features leading to model predictions.
Train specifically sparse models to have interpretable computations.
papers.abstract: Large data-driven physics models like DeepMind's weather model GraphCast have empirically succeeded in parameterizing time operators for complex dynamical systems with an accuracy reaching or in some cases exceeding that of traditional physics-based solvers. Unfortunately, how these data-driven models perform computations is largely unknown and whether their internal representations are interpretable or physically consistent is an open question. Here, we adapt tools from interpretability research in Large Language Models to analyze intermediate computational layers in GraphCast, leveraging sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable features in the neuron space of the model. We uncover distinct features on a wide range of length and time scales that correspond to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal behavior, large-scale precipitation patterns, specific geographical coding, and sea-ice extent, among others. We further demonstrate how the precise abstraction of these features can be probed via interventions on the prediction steps of the model. As a case study, we sparsely modify a feature corresponding to tropical cyclones in GraphCast and observe interpretable and physically consistent modifications to evolving hurricanes. Such methods offer a window into the black-box behavior of data-driven physics models and are a step towards realizing their potential as trustworthy predictors and scientifically valuable tools for discovery.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Explanatory models in neuroscience: Part 1 -- taking mechanistic abstraction seriously
papers.research_question: What criteria must neural network models satisfy to be considered mechanistic explanations of brain function?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the 3M++ criteria, which expand the notion of model-to-mechanism mapping to show that deep neural networks can serve as abstract mechanistic models of brain function when they are runnable and mappable via similarity transforms.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks can be good mechanistic models of brain function when assessed with the 3M++ criteria, and the appropriate level of abstraction is key to their explanatory power.
papers.key_findings:
The 3M++ criteria require a model to be a 'runnable abstraction' and to be mappable to the brain using similarity transforms (like linear transforms).
Deep neural networks, when trained for object recognition, can satisfy the 3M++ criteria and thus serve as mechanistic models of the primate ventral visual pathway.
The abstractions used in DNNs (e.g., Linear-Nonlinear units) are the same as those already employed in experimental neuroscience.
The mapping between DNN layers and brain areas can be performed using linear transforms, analogous to mapping neural responses across individuals.
The level of abstraction is crucial; DNNs operate at the spike-rate level, which is a self-consistent and predictively adequate level for explaining visual processing.
papers.limitation: HCNNs do not explain 100% of the stimulus-driven variability of ventral pathway neurons, up to the inter-animal noise ceiling.
future_direction: Developing improved models (e.g., with recurrent and feedback connections) to achieve 100% statistical accuracy in mapping to the visual system.
Exploring the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, as addressed in the companion paper.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of neural network models in mimicking animal performance on visual perceptual tasks, critics worry that these models fail to illuminate brain function. We take it that a central approach to explanation in systems neuroscience is that of mechanistic modeling, where understanding the system is taken to require fleshing out the parts, organization, and activities of a system, and how those give rise to behaviors of interest. However, it remains somewhat controversial what it means for a model to describe a mechanism, and whether neural network models qualify as explanatory. We argue that certain kinds of neural network models are actually good examples of mechanistic models, when the right notion of mechanistic mapping is deployed. Building on existing work on model-to-mechanism mapping (3M), we describe criteria delineating such a notion, which we call 3M++. These criteria require us, first, to identify a level of description that is both abstract but detailed enough to be "runnable", and then, to construct model-to-brain mappings using the same principles as those employed for brain-to-brain mapping across individuals. Perhaps surprisingly, the abstractions required are those already in use in experimental neuroscience, and are of the kind deployed in the construction of more familiar computational models, just as the principles of inter-brain mappings are very much in the spirit of those already employed in the collection and analysis of data across animals. In a companion paper, we address the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, in the context of functional evolutionary explanations. Taken together, mechanistic interpretations of computational models and the dependencies between form and function illuminated by optimization processes can help us to understand why brain systems are built they way they are.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Toward Knowledge Extraction in Classification of Volcano-Seismic Events: Visualizing Hidden States in Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we understand what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model in the context of volcano-seismic event classification, and how can this knowledge be used to improve data interpretation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces visualization approaches to understand the hidden state dynamics of RNNs in volcano-seismic event classification, showing how neuron specialization varies with architecture and event type, and how this can be used for network pruning and active learning.
papers.conclusion: The visualization approaches help understand RNN internal mechanisms, and neuron specialization can be used for network pruning and active learning in volcano-seismic event classification.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM architectures exhibit lower neuronal activity and better specialization compared to Vanilla RNN.
Neurons specialize for specific events and frequency bands, which can be visualized through activation maps.
The degree of specialization allows for network pruning (removing less specialized neurons) without significant performance loss.
LSTM architectures are more stable and have higher susceptibility to changes in input compared to Vanilla RNN.
future_direction: Exploring the correlation between dropout and specialization of neurons.
Using neuron specialization for active learning and network sparsity.
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep hierarchical models build their knowledge is a key issue in the usage of artificial intelligence to interpret the reality behind data. Depending on the discipline and models used, such knowledge may be represented in ways that are more or less intelligible for humans, limiting further improvements on the performance of the existing models. In order to delve into the characterization and modeling of volcano-seismic signals, this article emphasizes the idea of deciphering what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model, and how this knowledge can be used to improve data interpretation. The key to accomplishing these objectives is both analyzing the hidden state dynamics associated with their hidden units as well as pruning/trimming based on the specialization of neurons. In this article, we process, analyze, and visualize the hidden states activation maps of two RNN architectures when managing different types of volcano-seismic events. As a result, the class-dependent discriminative behavior of most active neurons is analyzed, thereby increasing the comprehension of the detection and classification tasks. A representative dataset from the deception island volcano (Antarctica), containing volcano-tectonic earthquakes, long period events, volcanic tremors, and hybrid events, is used to train the models. Experimental analysis shows how neural activity and its associated specialization skills change depending on the architecture chosen and the type of event analyzed.

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: Testing the Tools of Systems Neuroscience on Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Are the common analysis tools of systems neuroscience effective at identifying phenomena of interest, and can artificial neural networks serve as a suitable testing ground for these tools?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that artificial neural networks (ANNs) are an appropriate testing ground for the tools of systems neuroscience and provides a roadmap for performing such testing to evaluate the tools' utility in achieving mechanistic understanding.
papers.conclusion: ANNs are appropriate systems for vetting the tools of systems neuroscience; applying these tools to ANNs and explicitly testing the insights they provide will determine their utility and encourage more explicit definitions of the field's goals.
future_direction: Testing existing systems neuroscience tools on artificial neural networks with different architectures and tasks.
Developing new analysis methods based on gaps identified through testing.
Encouraging explicit definitions of what constitutes understanding in neuroscience.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists apply a range of common analysis tools to recorded neural activity in order to glean insights into how neural circuits implement computations. Despite the fact that these tools shape the progress of the field as a whole, we have little empirical evidence that they are effective at quickly identifying the phenomena of interest. Here I argue that these tools should be explicitly tested and that artificial neural networks (ANNs) are an appropriate testing grounds for them. The recent resurgence of the use of ANNs as models of everything from perception to memory to motor control stems from a rough similarity between artificial and biological neural networks and the ability to train these networks to perform complex high-dimensional tasks. These properties, combined with the ability to perfectly observe and manipulate these systems, makes them well-suited for vetting the tools of systems and cognitive neuroscience. I provide here both a roadmap for performing this testing and a list of tools that are suitable to be tested on ANNs. Using ANNs to reflect on the extent to which these tools provide a productive understanding of neural systems -- and on exactly what understanding should mean here -- has the potential to expedite progress in the study of the brain.

papers.title: Exploring Representations and Interventions in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how time series foundation models organize knowledge, what interpretable concepts they learn, and how to steer their predictions using conceptual priors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for analyzing and intervening in time series foundation models, including representation similarity analysis for pruning, concept identification, and steering predictions with conceptual priors.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges representational analysis from language and vision models to TSFMs, offering new methods for building more computationally efficient and transparent time series foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger TSFMs exhibit block-like redundancy in representations, which can be leveraged for pruning to improve inference efficiency without significant performance loss.
TSFMs learn intuitive linear concepts (e.g., periodicity, trend) that are localized in specific layers and tokens.
It is possible to steer model predictions by intervening in the latent representations along conceptual directions, enabling concept-informed predictions without additional training.
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) promise to be powerful tools for a wide range of applications. However, their internal representations and learned concepts are still not well understood. In this study, we investigate the structure and redundancy of representations across various TSFMs, examining the self-similarity of model layers within and across different model sizes. This analysis reveals block-like redundancy in the representations, which can be utilized for informed pruning to improve inference speed and efficiency. Additionally, we explore the concepts learned by these models - such as periodicity and trends - and how these can be manipulated through latent space steering to influence model behavior. Our experiments show that steering interventions can introduce new features, e.g., adding periodicity or trends to signals that initially lacked them. These findings underscore the value of representational analysis for optimizing models and demonstrate how conceptual steering offers new possibilities for more controlled and efficient time series analysis with TSFMs.

papers.title: The Dynamics of Neural Populations Capture the Laws of the Mind
papers.research_question: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? The paper investigates how the dynamics of neural populations can capture the laws of the mind.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that neural population dynamics, described as attractor states in low-dimensional feature spaces, form a privileged level of description for cognition, where macroscopic patterns enslave microscopic neural activity, and that networks of such dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures.
papers.conclusion: The dynamics of neural populations form a privileged level of description at which the laws of behavior and cognition manifest themselves, and this level cannot be eliminated by reduction to a more microscopic level.
papers.key_findings:
Neural populations are a privileged level of description to understand cognition and behavior.
Neural dynamics at the population level generate stable attractor states that serve as representations.
Cognition unfolds as sequences of stable neural states are autonomously generated by neural dynamical systems that go through instabilities.
Networks of neural dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures that enable increasingly complex forms of cognition.
The reduction of mind to neural mechanisms should follow the non-equilibrium physics metaphor, where macroscopic neural states enslave microscopic neural activity.
papers.limitation:
The separation of scales between macroscopic neural dynamics and microscopic neural activity might be broken by complex nonlinear processes that reach across spatial and temporal scales.
The paper does not cover how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
future_direction: Address how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
Explore scale-free theories that avoid reductive elimination of the macroscopic scale.
papers.abstract: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? Neural accounts of the mind are often sought in a reductionistic spirit in which neural mechanisms explain cognition. Because an individual's thoughts and behaviors are not reproducible without careful control of task, stimulus, and behavioral history, laws of the mind are the currency of psychology. Reduction may thus have to take the form familiar from physics: deriving macroscopic laws from microscopic laws. I argue that the metaphor of reduction from non-equilibrium physics may be the most appropriate. Macroscopic patterns of neural activity, which cause behavior and thought, are slow dynamical variables that dominate the fast microscopic dynamics of individual neurons and synapses. I outline a theoretical framework in which strongly recurrent neural networks, described by neural dynamics, generate neural representations as attractor states that are embedded in low-dimensional feature spaces. Instabilities of these states are instrumental in decision-making and the generation of sequences of mental states that are the basis for higher cognition. Networks of such neural population dynamics form neural cognitive architectures that capture the laws of the mind.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context
papers.research_question: How do transformers perform in-context learning of dynamical systems, and what mechanisms enable them to forecast unseen physical systems without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on dynamical systems learn to perform time-delay embedding and approximate transfer operators in-context, enabling out-of-distribution generalization to unseen systems.
papers.conclusion: Transformers extract a system-independent forecasting strategy by performing time-delay embedding and approximating transfer operators in-context, explaining their ability to generalize to unseen dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
An early tradeoff between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance manifests as a secondary double descent phenomenon during training.
Transformers adaptively perform time-delay embedding during inference to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the input system's attractor.
Transformers learn to approximate the Perron-Frobenius (transfer) operator of the fully-observed system in-context, capturing its dominant timescales and metastable states.
Out-of-distribution generalization error scales linearly with the KL divergence between the training and testing system attractors.
The effective order of the Markov chain approximating the transformer's dynamics scales linearly with the intrinsic dimension of the test system's attractor, consistent with Takens' theorem.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models for scientific machine learning adapt to physical settings unseen during training, such as zero-shot transfer between turbulent scales. This phenomenon, in-context learning, challenges conventional understanding of learning and adaptation in physical systems. Here, we study in-context learning of dynamical systems in a minimal setting: we train a small two-layer, single-head transformer to forecast one dynamical system, and then evaluate its ability to forecast a different dynamical system without retraining. We discover an early tradeoff in training between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance, which manifests as a secondary double descent phenomenon. We discover that attention-based models apply a transfer-operator forecasting strategy in-context. They (1) lift low-dimensional time series using delay embedding, to detect the system's higher-dimensional dynamical manifold, and (2) identify and forecast long-lived invariant sets that characterize the global flow on this manifold. Our results clarify the mechanism enabling large pretrained models to forecast unseen physical systems at test without retraining, and they illustrate the unique ability of attention-based models to leverage global attractor information in service of short-term forecasts.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
Cholinergic modulation is a common mechanism that biases processing toward external modes across multiple systems.
future_direction: Test the prediction that disruption of mode-switching (e.g., between non-REM and REM sleep) impairs integration of new hippocampal memories with existing neocortical knowledge.
Investigate how altering the timescale of switching affects the learning of temporally extended features.
Explore the role of neuromodulators like acetylcholine in regulating mode-switching and learning across different brain systems.
papers.abstract: Brains construct internal models that support perception, prediction, and action in the external world. Individual circuits within a brain also learn internal models of the local world of input they receive, in order to facilitate efficient and robust representation. How are these internal models learned? We propose that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing. We review computational evidence that this mode-switching can produce an error signal to drive learning. We then consider empirical evidence for the instantiation of mode-switching in diverse neural systems, ranging from subsecond fluctuations in the hippocampus to wake-sleep alternations across the whole brain. We hypothesize that these internal/external switching processes, which occur at multiple scales, can drive learning at each scale. This framework predicts that (a) slower mode-switching should be associated with learning of more temporally extended input features and (b) disruption of switching should impair the integration of new information with prior information.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Model discovery to link neural activity to behavioral tasks
papers.research_question: How can we discover and characterize models that relate task features (sensory stimuli, behavioral actions, internal states) to neural activity without relying on predefined models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MINE, a framework using CNNs to discover models linking task features to neural activity, with interpretability achieved through Taylor decomposition to characterize computational complexity and receptive fields.
papers.conclusion: MINE provides a flexible and interpretable framework for model discovery in neuroscience, enabling the characterization of neural encoding without a priori assumptions, and has been successfully applied to identify novel neuron classes.
papers.key_findings:
MINE can capture diverse linear and nonlinear relationships between predictors and neural activity, outperforming simple linear regression.
Taylor decomposition allows quantification of computational complexity, distinguishing linear from nonlinear neural processing.
MINE can extract linear and nonlinear receptive fields, similar to Volterra kernel analysis, even on naturalistic stimuli.
Applied to zebrafish data, MINE identified neurons with specific receptive fields and computational complexities that anatomically segregate.
Discovered a new class of neurons integrating thermosensory and behavioral information that was missed by traditional methods.
future_direction: Extend MINE to joint population encoding and analysis
Incorporate neural population activity as predictors
Improve model-fitting efficiency
papers.abstract: Brains are not engineered solutions to a well-defined problem but arose through selective pressure acting on random variation. It is therefore unclear how well a model chosen by an experimenter can relate neural activity to experimental conditions. Here, we developed 'model identification of neural encoding (MINE).' MINE is an accessible framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to discover and characterize a model that relates aspects of tasks to neural activity. Although flexible, CNNs are difficult to interpret. We use Taylor decomposition approaches to understand the discovered model and how it maps task features to activity. We apply MINE to a published cortical dataset as well as experiments designed to probe thermoregulatory circuits in zebrafish. Here, MINE allowed us to characterize neurons according to their receptive field and computational complexity, features that anatomically segregate in the brain. We also identified a new class of neurons that integrate thermosensory and behavioral information that eluded us previously when using traditional clustering and regression-based approaches.

papers.title: FIGNN: Feature-Specific Interpretability for Graph Neural Network Surrogate Models
papers.research_question: How can we design a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that provides feature-specific interpretability for multivariate prediction tasks on unstructured grids in scientific applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-specific interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN) architecture with independent Top-K pooling masks per output variable and an error-budget regularization term to align interpretability with predictive error, enabling localized, feature-wise attribution in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.conclusion: FIGNN provides a balance between interpretability and predictive performance, offering domain experts detailed insights into feature-specific contributions to prediction accuracy in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.key_findings:
FIGNN provides feature-specific interpretability masks that highlight physically meaningful spatial regions for each predicted variable, such as frontal boundaries in climate data and recirculation zones in fluid flow.
The error budget regularization effectively localizes prediction errors within the masked regions, with stronger regularization increasing error concentration at the cost of slightly reduced predictive accuracy.
FIGNN maintains competitive predictive performance compared to baseline GNN models on both atmospheric (SPEEDY) and fluid dynamics (BFS) datasets.
The method generalizes across distinct physical domains (climate and fluid dynamics) with different mesh types and governing equations.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence and error localization) and predictive accuracy, controllable via the regularization parameter λ.
papers.limitation:
Error accumulation in multi-step rollouts leads to deteriorating prediction quality over long time horizons.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence) and predictive accuracy, where higher regularization improves error localization but increases final loss.
future_direction: Extending the framework to spatially three-dimensional settings.
Real-time adaptive interpretability.
Uncertainty quantification strategies.
Using FIGNN for inverse problems like super-resolution, control, and optimization.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel graph neural network (GNN) architecture, the Feature-specific Interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN), designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning surrogate models defined on unstructured grids in scientific applications. Traditional GNNs often obscure the distinct spatial influences of different features in multivariate prediction tasks. FIGNN addresses this limitation by introducing a feature-specific pooling strategy, which enables independent attribution of spatial importance for each predicted variable. Additionally, a mask-based regularization term is incorporated into the training objective to explicitly encourage alignment between interpretability and predictive error, promoting localized attribution of model performance. The method is evaluated for surrogate modeling of two physically distinct systems: the SPEEDY atmospheric circulation model and the backward-facing step (BFS) fluid dynamics benchmark. Results demonstrate that FIGNN achieves competitive predictive performance while revealing physically meaningful spatial patterns unique to each feature. Analysis of rollout stability, feature-wise error budgets, and spatial mask overlays confirm the utility of FIGNN as a general-purpose framework for interpretable surrogate modeling in complex physical domains.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Identification of state functions by physically-guided neural networks with physically-meaningful internal layers
papers.research_question: How to predict the input-output relation in a physical system while fulfilling physical constraints, and how to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Physically-Guided Neural Networks with Internal Variables (PGNNIV), a method that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to predict system behavior and infer internal state variables, showing improved convergence, data efficiency, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: PGNNIV is a promising framework that combines the predictive power of neural networks with physical interpretability, and shows advantages over standard neural networks in terms of convergence, data needs, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.key_findings:
The method accelerates the training process.
It reduces the amount of data required for similar accuracy.
It filters noise in experimental data.
It provides improved extrapolation capacity.
It allows obtaining internal state variables without additional assumptions.
papers.limitation:
For deep neural models, large and varied data are needed.
Defining successful network topology and hyperparameters is complex and time-consuming.
Predictions may not be as accurate as using full prescribed mathematical models.
papers.abstract: Substitution of well-grounded theoretical models by data-driven predictions is not as simple in engineering and sciences as it is in social and economic fields. Scientific problems suffer most times from paucity of data, while they may involve a large number of variables and parameters that interact in complex and non-stationary ways, obeying certain physical laws. Moreover, a physically-based model is not only useful for making predictions, but to gain knowledge by the interpretation of its structure, parameters, and mathematical properties. The solution to these shortcomings seems to be the seamless blending of the tremendous predictive power of the data-driven approach with the scientific consistency and interpretability of physically-based models. We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Transformers for Dynamical Systems
papers.research_question: What are the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers for linear and nonlinear dynamical systems, and how do they relate to classical dynamical systems theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that softmax attention's convexity constraint limits representation of oscillatory linear dynamics, while for nonlinear systems with partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism enabling state reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The success of attention-based models in dynamical systems forecasting depends critically on the interplay between the system’s spectral properties, the observation regime, and the model’s architectural constraints.
papers.key_findings:
For linear systems, the convexity constraint of softmax attention restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings.
For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available.
Transformers can implicitly perform delay-coordinate embeddings, and the benefit of attention is most pronounced in partial observation regimes.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems and can lead to uniform averaging without them.
The latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding of the attractor.
papers.limitation:
Softmax normalization enforces non-negativity and convexity that restrict representable dynamics.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems.
Latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding before projection.
Analysis is limited to single-layer Transformers, and deeper architectures may exhibit different behaviors.
future_direction: Multi-head attention and multi-layer architectures to understand how multiple heads might specialize in distinct modes.
Mechanistic interpretability for stiff and multiscale systems to see if attention offers advantages in adaptive integration.
Shared latent space geometry in foundation models to understand how distinct dynamical behaviors are embedded.
papers.abstract: Transformers are increasingly adopted for modeling and forecasting time-series, yet their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood from a dynamical systems perspective. In contrast to classical autoregressive and state-space models, which benefit from well-established theoretical foundations, Transformer architectures are typically treated as black boxes. This gap becomes particularly relevant as attention-based models are considered for general-purpose or zero-shot forecasting across diverse dynamical regimes. In this work, we do not propose a new forecasting model, but instead investigate the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers when applied to dynamical data. Building on a dynamical systems perspective we interpret causal self-attention as a linear, history-dependent recurrence and analyze how it processes temporal information. Through a series of linear and nonlinear case studies, we identify distinct operational regimes. For linear systems, we show that the convexity constraint imposed by softmax attention fundamentally restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings. For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention instead acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available. These results help bridge empirical observations with classical dynamical systems theory, providing insight into when and why Transformers succeed or fail as models of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
