This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Interpretability of artificial neural network models in artificial Intelligence vs. neuroscience
papers.research_question: What are the different notions of interpretability in artificial intelligence and neuroscience, and how can neuroscientific interpretability be pursued independently?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that interpretability in AI and neuroscience are distinct, with neuroscientific interpretability requiring alignment between model components and brain constructs, and proposes that brain alignment can serve as a benchmark for evaluating AI explainability methods.
papers.conclusion: The authors encourage researchers to conceptually separate the objectives of AI and neuroscience interpretability, but suggest that AI interpretability methods aligned with primate brain interpretations are more promising.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-faceted construct used differently in AI (focusing on model component contributions to output) and neuroscience (requiring alignment with brain constructs).
Neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs is relative and depends on the model's intended use and the grain of analysis, with no need for full brain alignment if only specific experimental variables are of interest.
Current ANN models of primate vision contain features not mapped to neuroscientific constructs, limiting their neuroscientific interpretability.
Brain alignment (similarity with primate behavior and neural measurements) can validate the 'goodness' of AI explainability methods in the absence of ground truth.
AI interpretability methods that provide more primate-brain-aligned model interpretations are likely more promising, despite operational differences from brains.
papers.abstract: Computationally explicit hypotheses of brain function derived from machine learning (ML)-based models have recently revolutionized neuroscience. Despite the unprecedented ability of these artificial neural networks (ANNs) to capture responses in biological neural networks (brains), and our full access to all internal model components (unlike the brain), ANNs are often referred to as black-boxes with limited interpretability. Interpretability, however, is a multi-faceted construct that is used differently across fields. In particular, interpretability, or explainability, efforts in Artificial Intelligence (AI) focus on understanding how different model components contribute to its output (i.e., decision making). In contrast, the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs requires explicit alignment between model components and neuroscientific constructs (e.g., different brain areas or phenomena, like recurrence or top-down feedback). Given the widespread calls to improve the interpretability of AI systems, we here highlight these different notions of interpretability and argue that the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs can be pursued in parallel with, but independently from, the ongoing efforts in AI. Certain ML techniques (e.g., deep dream) can be leveraged in both fields, to ask what stimulus optimally activates the specific model features (feature visualization by optimization), or how different features contribute to the model's output (feature attribution). However, without appropriate brain alignment, certain features will remain uninterpretable to neuroscientists.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Expressive dynamics models with nonlinear injective readouts enable reliable recovery of latent features from neural activity
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable latent dynamical systems from neural activity? The paper proposes that using injective nonlinear readouts in neural population dynamics models can prevent the model from inventing latent features not reflected in the data, leading to more interpretable dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ODIN, a neural population dynamics model with an injective nonlinear readout, which learns interpretable latent dynamical systems from neural activity by preventing the invention of misleading latent features and enabling accurate recovery of ground-truth dynamics.
papers.conclusion: ODIN is a promising method for distilling interpretable dynamics from neural activity, enabling better understanding of neural computation.
papers.key_findings:
ODIN with injective nonlinear readout recovers latent activity more accurately than linear or MLP readouts, especially when the latent dimensionality is overestimated.
Linear and MLP readouts tend to be non-injective, allowing latent features that do not affect neural activity, which degrades interpretability.
ODIN can recover nonlinear embeddings and fixed point structures from synthetic data.
On biological neural data, ODIN reconstructs neural activity with fewer latent dimensions than linear readout models and performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.limitation:
ODIN is not yet able to account for inputs to the system that may be coming from areas that are not directly modeled, so it models the dynamics as an autonomous system.
Human neural interfaces combined with an understanding of neural computation might lead to strategies that are effective at influencing behavior, which could be misused.
future_direction: Developing methods for input inference in NODE-based models.
Focusing on applications of this research that are scientific and medical rather than commercial or political.
papers.abstract: The advent of large-scale neural recordings has enabled new methods to discover the computational mechanisms of neural circuits by understanding the rules that govern how their state evolves over time. While these \textit{neural dynamics} cannot be directly measured, they can typically be approximated by low-dimensional models in a latent space. How these models represent the mapping from latent space to neural space can affect the interpretability of the latent representation. We show that typical choices for this mapping (e.g., linear or MLP) often lack the property of injectivity, meaning that changes in latent state are not obligated to affect activity in the neural space. During training, non-injective readouts incentivize the invention of dynamics that misrepresent the underlying system and the computation it performs. Combining our injective Flow readout with prior work on interpretable latent dynamics models, we created the Ordinary Differential equations autoencoder with Injective Nonlinear readout (ODIN), which captures latent dynamical systems that are nonlinearly embedded into observed neural activity via an approximately injective nonlinear mapping. We show that ODIN can recover nonlinearly embedded systems from simulated neural activity, even when the nature of the system and embedding are unknown. Additionally, ODIN enables the unsupervised recovery of underlying dynamical features (e.g., fixed points) and embedding geometry. When applied to biological neural recordings, ODIN can reconstruct neural activity with comparable accuracy to previous state-of-the-art methods while using substantially fewer latent dimensions. Overall, ODIN's accuracy in recovering ground-truth latent features and ability to accurately reconstruct neural activity with low dimensionality make it a promising method for distilling interpretable dynamics that can help explain neural computation.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Neural Earthquake Forecasting with Minimal Information: Limits, Interpretability, and the Role of Markov Structure
papers.research_question: Can neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting generalize temporally when trained on early data and tested on future unseen events?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hybrid neural-Markov model for earthquake forecasting and a temporal cross-validation framework, showing that model performance degrades on future data due to non-stationarity, highlighting the importance of temporal evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting fail to generalize to future data due to temporal non-stationarity, highlighting the need for temporally realistic evaluation and caution in applying machine learning to sparse forecasting settings.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model outperforms the Markov baseline on validation data but fails to generalize to the most recent quintile of the catalog.
The final quintile of seismicity exhibits more Markov-consistent behavior than earlier data, indicating temporal non-stationarity.
Integrated Gradients attribution shows a shift in feature importance between validation and test sets, with magnitude features becoming more relevant in the test set.
Temporal cross-validation reveals that model performance is highly dependent on the temporal location of the test data, with the last quintile consistently underperforming.
The study underscores the risk of overfitting to early patterns and the need for temporally realistic benchmarks in earthquake forecasting.
papers.limitation:
Small sample size affects all statistical models based on this data.
Sparse input features limited to simple descriptors of past events restrict the models' ability to capture complex physical dynamics.
The Markov prior is static and unable to account for possible changes in seismic regimes.
Results are based on a single regional earthquake catalog without additional geophysical or contextual data.
Only feedforward architectures were considered; models with more explicit temporal reasoning were not explored.
future_direction: Refine the use of prior knowledge with dynamic extensions of the Markov model or hierarchical priors that adapt across segments of the catalog.
Incorporate additional physical variables such as fault-specific information, geodetic signals, or stress evolution proxies.
Explore dynamically updated models or time-aware architectures to track evolving patterns more effectively.
papers.abstract: Abstract Forecasting earthquake sequences remains a central challenge in seismology, particularly under non-stationary conditions. While deep learning models have shown promise, their ability to generalize across time remains poorly understood. We evaluate neural and hybrid (NN + Markov) models for short-term earthquake forecasting on a regional catalog using temporally stratified cross-validation. Models are trained on earlier portions of the catalog and evaluated on future unseen events, enabling realistic assessment of temporal generalization. We find that while these models outperform a purely Markovian model on validation data, their test performance degrades substantially in the most recent quintile. A detailed attribution analysis reveals a shift in feature relevance over time, with later data exhibiting simpler, more Markov-consistent behavior. To support interpretability, we apply Integrated Gradients, a type of explainable AI (XAI) to analyze how models rely on different input features. These results highlight the risks of overfitting to early patterns in seismicity and underscore the importance of temporally realistic benchmarks. We conclude that forecasting skill is inherently time-dependent and benefits from combining physical priors with data-driven methods.

papers.title: Trainability, Expressivity and Interpretability in Gated Neural ODEs
papers.research_question: Can we improve performance of neural ODEs by introducing gating interactions? How does the structure of the neural network modeling the velocity flow field influence a nODE's capacity to model complex trajectories? Does the capability of low-dimensional nODEs to model complex data improve interpretability of the dynamical computation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces gated neural ODEs (gnODEs) which improve trainability, expressivity, and interpretability of neural ODEs by incorporating gating interactions that provide adaptive timescales and inductive bias for continuous attractors.
papers.conclusion: Gated neural ODEs combine the benefits of gating (adaptive timescales, improved trainability) with the expressivity and interpretability of neural ODEs, making them powerful for dynamical modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Gating improves trainability of nODEs on tasks involving long timescales.
gnODEs are more expressive than RNNs in many parameter regimes, especially in low dimensions.
gnODEs exhibit an inductive bias to utilize marginally-stable fixed points (continuous attractors) for memory tasks.
Reduced-dimensional gnODEs are interpretable, allowing visualization of learned attractor structures.
Gating benefits nODEs on real-world tasks like character trajectory classification and speech commands.
future_direction: Incorporating gating interactions more directly in neural controlled differential equations (nCDEs).
Exploring interactions between gating and linear-nonlinear decompositions in RNN architectures.
Making the timescale τ trainable in gnODEs to potentially improve performance.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the dynamics in biological and artificial neural networks implement the computations required for a task is a salient open question in machine learning and neuroscience. In particular, computations requiring complex memory storage and retrieval pose a significant challenge for these networks to implement or learn. Recently, a family of models described by neural ordinary differential equations (nODEs) has emerged as powerful dynamical neural network models capable of capturing complex dynamics. Here, we extend nODEs by endowing them with adaptive timescales using gating interactions. We refer to these as gated neural ODEs (gnODEs). Using a task that requires memory of continuous quantities, we demonstrate the inductive bias of the gnODEs to learn (approximate) continuous attractors. We further show how reduced-dimensional gnODEs retain their modeling power while greatly improving interpretability, even allowing explicit visualization of the structure of learned attractors. We introduce a novel measure of expressivity which probes the capacity of a neural network to generate complex trajectories. Using this measure, we explore how the phase-space dimension of the nODEs and the complexity of the function modeling the flow field contribute to expressivity. We see that a more complex function for modeling the flow field allows a lower-dimensional nODE to capture a given target dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of gating in nODEs on several real-world tasks.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: How Much of a Model Do We Need? Redundancy and Slimmability in Remote Sensing Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do remote sensing foundation models enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than computer vision models, and do they rely on redundant representations?
papers.core_contribution: Remote sensing foundation models exhibit high post-hoc slimmability, retaining over 71% relative accuracy at 1% compute due to redundant representations, contrasting sharply with computer vision models.
papers.conclusion: RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than CV models, with redundant representations enabling high slimmability, making post-hoc slimming a practical tool for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.key_findings:
RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at 1% computational budget across all models and tasks, a sevenfold improvement over CV models.
Learned slimmable training improves MoCo-based models but not MAE-based models, with MoCo showing advantages at low scales.
Feature correlation analysis reveals distinct scaling strategies: DOFA shows organized to independent features, Prithvi shows U-shaped patterns, and TerraMind shows monotonic decrease.
Explained variance ratio indicates that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy, leading to robust slimmability.
Intermediate-scale deployment often achieves superior accuracy through implicit regularization, offering up to 12x speedups.
future_direction: Develop slimmable training techniques for MAE's reconstruction objective.
Investigate modality-specific compression tolerances.
Explore non-uniform slimming strategies.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models (FMs) in remote sensing (RS) are developed based on the paradigms established in computer vision (CV) and have shown promise for various Earth observation applications. However, the direct transfer of scaling assumptions from CV to RS has not been adequately examined. We hypothesize that RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at substantially smaller scales than their CV counterparts, where increasing parameter count primarily induces redundant representations rather than qualitatively new abstractions. To test this hypothesis, we use post-hoc slimming, where we uniformly reduce the width of pretrained encoder, as a tool to measure representational redundancy across six state-of-the-art RS FMs on four downstream classification tasks. Our findings reveal a significant contrast with those in the CV domain: while a post-hoc slimmed masked autoencoder (MAE) trained on ImageNet retains less than 10% accuracy at 1% FLOPs, RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at the same budget. This sevenfold difference provides strong empirical support for our hypothesis. We further demonstrate that learned slimmable training can improve both Momentum Contrast (MoCo)- and MAE- based models. In addition, through the explained variance ratio and the feature correlation analysis, we provide mechanistic explanations showing that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy. Our findings establish post-hoc slimmability as both a practical deployment strategy for resource-constrained environments and a diagnostic tool that challenges the prevailing scaling paradigm in RS. Upon acceptance, we will publish all code.

papers.title: Multilevel Interpretability Of Artificial Neural Networks: Leveraging Framework And Methods From Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can frameworks and methods from neuroscience, specifically Marr's levels of analysis, be leveraged to interpret artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilevel interpretability framework inspired by neuroscience, specifically Marr's three levels of analysis (computation, algorithm/representation, implementation), to provide a principled approach for understanding artificial neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The multilevel interpretability framework provides a principled way to tackle neural system complexity, links structure, computation, and behavior, and paves the way toward a unified effort for understanding intelligent systems, whether biological or artificial.
papers.limitation: Differences between biological and artificial neural systems may limit the direct application of neuroscience methods and frameworks to AI interpretability.
future_direction: Applying the multilevel framework to specific behaviors like deception in AI systems.
Further integration of neuroscience and AI interpretability research.
Developing benchmarks and theoretical models for behaviors like deception at the computational level.
papers.abstract: As deep learning systems are scaled up to many billions of parameters, relating their internal structure to external behaviors becomes very challenging. Although daunting, this problem is not new: Neuroscientists and cognitive scientists have accumulated decades of experience analyzing a particularly complex system - the brain. In this work, we argue that interpreting both biological and artificial neural systems requires analyzing those systems at multiple levels of analysis, with different analytic tools for each level. We first lay out a joint grand challenge among scientists who study the brain and who study artificial neural networks: understanding how distributed neural mechanisms give rise to complex cognition and behavior. We then present a series of analytical tools that can be used to analyze biological and artificial neural systems, organizing those tools according to Marr's three levels of analysis: computation/behavior, algorithm/representation, and implementation. Overall, the multilevel interpretability framework provides a principled way to tackle neural system complexity; links structure, computation, and behavior; clarifies assumptions and research priorities at each level; and paves the way toward a unified effort for understanding intelligent systems, may they be biological or artificial.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Autoregressive Deep Learning: Or, Examining Temporal Decay of Gradient Coherence
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish between genuine generalization and mere memorization in autoregressive PDE emulators? What are the limitations of standard models and training routines in achieving generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces influence-based diagnostics to show that autoregressive PDE emulators fail to learn a globally consistent solution operator, instead memorizing time- and class-specific patterns, and provides insights for improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current physics-agnostic PDE emulators fail to internalize the governing equations, and influence functions provide a diagnostic framework to distinguish memorization from generalization, highlighting the need for physics-based constraints or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive PDE emulators exhibit rapid decay of off-diagonal influence, indicating gradient responses are localized in time and class.
Both UNet and ViT models fail to support nontrivial off-diagonal response, meaning they do not learn a shared feature basis across trajectories.
Gradient geometry is class-locked, with limited inter-class influence, showing that models treat different initial conditions as separate tasks.
The neural tangent kernel spectrum reveals a stiff, anisotropic geometry, indicating that low test error coexists with sharp, high-curvature directions rather than robust generalization.
The models behave as statistical estimators that interpolate within neighborhoods of the training data, rather than learning the underlying physical laws.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based constraints as regularizers or architectural biases to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained as autoregressive PDE surrogates hold significant promise for accelerating scientific discovery through their capacity to both extrapolate beyond training regimes and efficiently adapt to downstream tasks despite a paucity of examples for fine-tuning. However, reliably achieving genuine generalization - a necessary capability for producing novel scientific insights and robustly performing during deployment - remains a critical challenge. Establishing whether or not these requirements are met demands evaluation metrics capable of clearly distinguishing genuine model generalization from mere memorization. We apply the influence function formalism to systematically characterize how autoregressive PDE surrogates assimilate and propagate information derived from diverse physical scenarios, revealing fundamental limitations of standard models and training routines in addition to providing actionable insights regarding the design of improved surrogates.

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: From Kepler to Newton: Inductive Biases Guide Learned World Models in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn the Newtonian world model for planetary motion, and how can we fix this problem?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that three minimal inductive biases—spatial smoothness, spatial stability, and temporal locality—enable generic Transformers to learn Newtonian world models for planetary motion, transitioning from curve-fitting (Keplerian) to mechanistic (Newtonian) understanding.
papers.conclusion: Simple inductive biases (spatial smoothness, stability, and temporal locality) are necessary and sufficient for transformers to learn world models, and true scientific understanding requires discovering governing mechanisms rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization disrupts spatial smoothness and prevents the emergence of a high-quality spatial map in the embedding space.
Using continuous coordinates with noisy context learning (spatial stability) mitigates error accumulation and improves prediction accuracy over tokenized classification.
Short context lengths (temporal locality) induce Newtonian world models (force-based), while long context lengths induce Keplerian world models (geometry-based).
There is a phase transition between Keplerian and Newtonian world models as context length varies.
Regression models with continuous inputs outperform classification models with tokenization when hyperparameters are optimized.
papers.limitation:
The study simplified the setup of Vafa et al. by using one time-scale instead of two.
Linear probing only reveals implicit knowledge and requires knowing what to look for a priori; a fully autonomous 'AI Physicist' would need additional mechanisms for symbolic extraction.
papers.abstract: Can general-purpose AI architectures go beyond prediction to discover the physical laws governing the universe? True intelligence relies on "world models" -- causal abstractions that allow an agent to not only predict future states but understand the underlying governing dynamics. While previous "AI Physicist" approaches have successfully recovered such laws, they typically rely on strong, domain-specific priors that effectively "bake in" the physics. Conversely, Vafa et al. recently showed that generic Transformers fail to acquire these world models, achieving high predictive accuracy without capturing the underlying physical laws. We bridge this gap by systematically introducing three minimal inductive biases. We show that ensuring spatial smoothness (by formulating prediction as continuous regression) and stability (by training with noisy contexts to mitigate error accumulation) enables generic Transformers to surpass prior failures and learn a coherent Keplerian world model, successfully fitting ellipses to planetary trajectories. However, true physical insight requires a third bias: temporal locality. By restricting the attention window to the immediate past -- imposing the simple assumption that future states depend only on the local state rather than a complex history -- we force the model to abandon curve-fitting and discover Newtonian force representations. Our results demonstrate that simple architectural choices determine whether an AI becomes a curve-fitter or a physicist, marking a critical step toward automated scientific discovery.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Deconstructing Recurrence, Attention, and Gating: Investigating the transferability of Transformers and Gated Recurrent Neural Networks in forecasting of dynamical systems
papers.research_question: What are the key architectural components (gating, attention, recurrence) that enable forecasting accuracy in Transformers and RNNs, and how can they be combined to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural gating and attention improve RNNs, while recurrence harms Transformers, and that a hybrid architecture combining Recurrent Highway Networks with gating and attention performs best for spatiotemporal forecasting.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that core mechanisms like gating, attention, and recurrence should be treated as hyperparameters and tuned for each task, leading to improved forecasting performance, with the best architecture being a hybrid Recurrent Highway Network with gating and attention.
papers.key_findings:
Neural gating and attention improve the performance of standard RNNs in most forecasting tasks.
Adding recurrence to Transformers is detrimental to their forecasting performance.
A hybrid architecture integrating Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms emerges as the best performing model for high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting.
Transformers train faster than RNNs but RNNs achieve higher forecasting accuracy.
The effectiveness of gating mechanisms (coupled vs. uncoupled) is task-dependent.
papers.abstract: Machine learning architectures, including transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have revolutionized forecasting in applications ranging from text processing to extreme weather. Notably, advanced network architectures, tuned for applications such as natural language processing, are transferable to other tasks such as spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. However, there is a scarcity of ablation studies to illustrate the key components that enable this forecasting accuracy. The absence of such studies, although explainable due to the associated computational cost, intensifies the belief that these models ought to be considered as black boxes. In this work, we decompose the key architectural components of the most powerful neural architectures, namely gating and recurrence in RNNs, and attention mechanisms in transformers. Then, we synthesize and build novel hybrid architectures from the standard blocks, performing ablation studies to identify which mechanisms are effective for each task. The importance of considering these components as hyper-parameters that can augment the standard architectures is exhibited on various forecasting datasets, from the spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics of the multiscale Lorenz 96 system, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, as well as standard real world time-series benchmarks. A key finding is that neural gating and attention improves the performance of all standard RNNs in most tasks, while the addition of a notion of recurrence in transformers is detrimental. Furthermore, our study reveals that a novel, sparsely used, architecture which integrates Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms, emerges as the best performing architecture in high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Scalable Mechanistic Neural Networks for Differential Equations and Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the Mechanistic Neural Network to achieve linear time and space complexity with respect to sequence length while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-MNN, a reformulation of the Mechanistic Neural Network that reduces computational time and space complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear in sequence length while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-MNN addresses the scalability limitations of MNN by reducing complexities to linear in sequence length, retaining precision and enabling efficient modeling of long-term dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
S-MNN matches the precision of the original MNN across various benchmarks.
S-MNN reduces computational time and memory usage significantly, enabling handling of long sequences.
The reformulation eliminates slack variables and uses a banded matrix structure for efficient solving.
S-MNN demonstrates practical applicability on long-term climate data forecasting.
The solver is numerically stable and GPU-friendly, achieving linear scaling in time and memory.
papers.abstract: We propose Scalable Mechanistic Neural Network (S-MNN), an enhanced neural network framework designed for scientific machine learning applications involving long temporal sequences. By reformulating the original Mechanistic Neural Network (MNN) (Pervez et al., 2024), we reduce the computational time and space complexities from cubic and quadratic with respect to the sequence length, respectively, to linear. This significant improvement enables efficient modeling of long-term dynamics without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S-MNN matches the original MNN in precision while substantially reducing computational resources. Consequently, S-MNN can drop-in replace the original MNN in applications, providing a practical and efficient tool for integrating mechanistic bottlenecks into neural network models of complex dynamical systems. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/ScalableMNN.

papers.title: On the Impact of Knowledge Distillation for Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does knowledge distillation improve model interpretability in addition to model accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge distillation improves model interpretability by transferring class-similarity information from teacher to student, making activation maps more object-centric.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of models, and this improvement is consistent across different KD methods, datasets, and notions of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
KD increases the number of concept detectors (interpretability) compared to training from scratch.
KD improves interpretability by transferring class-similarity information, while label smoothing reduces interpretability.
The interpretability of student models improves as the amount of class-similarity information they learn increases.
Various KD methods (vanilla KD, AT, FT, CRD, SSKD, self-KD) all improve model interpretability.
KD improves interpretability across different datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR, MNIST, SST) and different interpretability measures (concept detectors, five-band-scores, DiffROAR, loss gradients).
future_direction: Determine whether KD can yield other useful results (e.g., model robustness).
Explore whether additional metrics can be used to measure model interpretability.
papers.abstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields.

papers.title: Building artificial neural circuits for domain-general cognition: a primer on brain-inspired systems-level architecture
papers.research_question: How can principles from the brain's systems-level architecture, specifically recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes, inform the design of artificial neural networks for domain-general cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews three brain-inspired architectural principles (global recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes) that could serve as inductive biases for building artificial neural networks capable of domain-general cognition.
papers.conclusion: A systems-level view of the brain, focusing on recurrence, communication, and rapid structural changes, can provide valuable guidance for building artificial intelligence that achieves domain-general problem-solving, and testing these principles in artificial systems may help understand biological cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The brain's Multiple Demand system uses global recurrence to integrate and broadcast information across distributed regions, a feature that may be necessary for domain-general cognition in artificial systems.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale networks can improve information flow between modules, which is crucial for complex multimodal systems.
Short-term topological changes (e.g., via local learning rules) enable flexible reconfiguration of neural circuits, supporting rapid adaptation and abstract problem-solving.
Current artificial neural networks lack these system-level properties, and incorporating them could enhance their flexibility and generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating global recurrent loops into artificial neural networks to enable widespread integration and broadcasting of abstract knowledge.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale modular networks to improve information flow between components.
Enabling short-term topological changes through local learning rules to allow rapid reconfiguration and flexible problem-solving.
papers.abstract: There is a concerted effort to build domain-general artificial intelligence in the form of universal neural network models with sufficient computational flexibility to solve a wide variety of cognitive tasks but without requiring fine-tuning on individual problem spaces and domains. To do this, models need appropriate priors and inductive biases, such that trained models can generalise to out-of-distribution examples and new problem sets. Here we provide an overview of the hallmarks endowing biological neural networks with the functionality needed for flexible cognition, in order to establish which features might also be important to achieve similar functionality in artificial systems. We specifically discuss the role of system-level distribution of network communication and recurrence, in addition to the role of short-term topological changes for efficient local computation. As machine learning models become more complex, these principles may provide valuable directions in an otherwise vast space of possible architectures. In addition, testing these inductive biases within artificial systems may help us to understand the biological principles underlying domain-general cognition.

papers.title: Emergence of Computational Structure in a Neural Network Physics Simulator
papers.research_question: How do computational structures (interpretable components) emerge in neural networks, and what are the mechanisms and best methods for detecting them?
papers.core_contribution: The emergence of computational structures (collision detection heads) in a transformer-like physics simulator is associated with degenerate geometry in the loss landscape and follows power law dynamics, suggesting these components are governed by a degenerate effective potential.
papers.conclusion: Computational structures in neural networks emerge with power law dynamics due to degenerate geometry in the loss landscape, and measuring the dynamics of network components can be an effective way to detect emerging structures.
papers.key_findings:
Collision detection heads emerge in the attention mechanism of the transformer-like model trained to simulate particle physics.
The emergence of these heads coincides with power law dynamics in the attention-distance correlation function.
The emergence is associated with changes in the local learning coefficient (LLC), indicating a degenerate geometry in the loss landscape near the head's parameters.
The dynamics of the attention-distance correlation can be used to detect the emergence of computational structures, and transitions between head variants are marked by changes in the power law exponent.
The results suggest that computational structures develop slowly (as power laws) and that early training is critical for their formation.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a specific model architecture and task (particle physics simulation), and the findings may not generalize to other architectures or tasks.
The estimation of the local learning coefficient (LLC) requires hyperparameter tuning and may not produce reliable results for all attention heads at all checkpoints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other model architectures and learning tasks to see if similar phenomena occur.
Investigate how the early development of certain structures affects the formation of later structures and the final performance of the network.
Explore the coupling between the neural network and the target physical system in more detail, especially in sequential data or reinforcement learning settings.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often have identifiable computational structures - components of the network which perform an interpretable algorithm or task - but the mechanisms by which these emerge and the best methods for detecting these structures are not well understood. In this paper we investigate the emergence of computational structure in a transformer-like model trained to simulate the physics of a particle system, where the transformer's attention mechanism is used to transfer information between particles. We show that (a) structures emerge in the attention heads of the transformer which learn to detect particle collisions, (b) the emergence of these structures is associated to degenerate geometry in the loss landscape, and (c) the dynamics of this emergence follows a power law.
